content: A percentile represents the value of a variable below which a certain percentage of observations fall. For instance, the 20th percentile is the value or score below which 20% of the observations are located. Percentiles and the related concept of percentile rank are frequently used in descriptive statistics and in reporting scores from norm-referenced tests. The 25th percentile is also referred to as the first quartile, while the 50th percentile is known as the median. Although there is no universally accepted definition of a percentile, most definitions yield similar results when the number of observations is large. One common definition involves calculating the rank ( n = frac{N}{100} cdot p + frac{1}{2} ), rounding to the nearest integer, and selecting the value corresponding to that rank. An alternative method, often used in various applications, employs linear interpolation between the two nearest ranks instead of rounding. For a dataset of ( N ) values ranked from smallest to largest, the percentile corresponding to the ( n )-th value can be defined as ( p_n = frac{100}{N} cdot (n frac{1}{2}) ). For example, if ( N = 5 ), the percentile corresponding to the third value is ( p_3 = frac{100}{5} cdot (3 frac{1}{2}) = 50 ). To calculate the value ( v ) corresponding to a given percentile ( p ), if ( p leq p_1 ) or ( p geq p_N ), the value ( v ) is taken as ( v_1 ) or ( v_N ), respectively. Otherwise, an integer ( k ) is identified such that ( p_k leq p leq p_{k+1} ), and the value is calculated as ( v = v_k + frac{N}{100} cdot (p p_k) cdot (v_{k+1} v_k) ). When ( p = 50 ), this formula yields the median. For even ( N ) and ( p = 25 ), the formula provides the median of the first half of the dataset. A weighted percentile is a variation where the percentage is calculated based on the total weight rather than the total number of observations. In most spreadsheet applications, there is no standard function for weighted percentiles. One method for calculating weighted percentiles extends the previously described approach. Let ( w_N ) represent the weights associated with the ( N ) sample values, and let ( S_n = sum_{k=1}^n w_k ) be the cumulative sum of these weights. The formulas are then generalized as ( p_n = frac{100}{S_N} cdot (S_n frac{w_n}{2}) ) and ( v = v_k + frac{p p_k}{p_{k+1} p_k} cdot (v_{k+1} v_k) ). The relationship between percentiles, deciles, and quartiles is as follows: ( P_{25} = Q_1 ) (first quartile) ( P_{50} = D_5 = Q_2 ) (median) ( P_{75} = Q_3 ) (third quartile) ( P_{100} = D_{10} = Q_4 ) (maximum value) ( P_{10} = D_1 ), ( P_{20} = D_2 ), ( P_{30} = D_3 ), ( P_{40} = D_4 ), ( P_{60} = D_6 ), ( P_{70} = D_7 ), ( P_{80} = D_8 ), ( P_{90} = D_9 ). Note: One quartile corresponds to 25 percentiles, while one decile equals 10 percentiles. Examples of percentile applications include: 1. Internet Service Providers (ISPs) often bill burstable internet bandwidth by using the 95th or 98th percentile. This method excludes the top 5% or 2% of bandwidth peaks in a month and charges based on the next highest rate. This approach ensures that infrequent peaks are ignored, resulting in fairer billing for customers. 2. Physicians frequently use weight and height percentiles for infants and children as indicators of relative health.
